reference.source: Smith & Tanagho's General Urology / Campbell-Walsh Urology
clinicalPearls: Urinary incontinence is any involuntary leakage of urine, and classifying the type guides management: stress, urgency, mixed, overflow, and functional (continuous) incontinence
Stress incontinence is leakage with raised intra-abdominal pressure (coughing, laughing, exertion) due to sphincter or pelvic floor weakness, common after childbirth and in men after prostatectomy
Urgency incontinence is leakage accompanied by a sudden compelling desire to void, usually from detrusor overactivity, and is part of the overactive bladder syndrome
Overflow incontinence is dribbling from a chronically distended, poorly emptying bladder, often due to outlet obstruction or an underactive detrusor, and must not be missed
A focused history, examination (including pelvic and neurological), a bladder (frequency-volume) diary, and post-void residual measurement usually clarify the type
First-line management of stress incontinence is pelvic floor muscle training, while urgency incontinence is treated with bladder training and antimuscarinic or beta-3 agonist therapy

Reversible contributors summarised by the DIAPPERS concept (delirium, infection, atrophic changes, pharmaceuticals, psychological, excess output, restricted mobility, stool impaction) should be sought and corrected
Surgical options such as mid-urethral slings or colposuspension are considered for stress incontinence, and intravesical botulinum toxin or neuromodulation for refractory urgency incontinence
reference.pathophysiology: Continence requires coordinated bladder storage at low pressure with a competent, closed outlet, governed by autonomic and somatic innervation. Stress incontinence arises from a weakened pelvic floor and urethral sphincter (from childbirth, ageing, or prostatic surgery) so that raised abdominal pressure overcomes closure. Urgency incontinence results from involuntary detrusor contractions (detrusor overactivity), which may be idiopathic or neurogenic. Overflow incontinence occurs when a chronically overdistended bladder leaks around an obstruction or fails to contract effectively, as in outlet obstruction or an underactive/neurogenic detrusor. Mixed incontinence combines these mechanisms.
additionalDifferentials: Overflow incontinence from obstruction or detrusor underactivity
Vesicovaginal or other urinary fistula (continuous leakage)
additionalInvestigations: Urinalysis to exclude infection and haematuria
Cough stress test and pelvic examination (assessing prolapse and pelvic floor)
Urodynamic studies in complex, mixed, or pre-surgical cases
Cystoscopy or imaging when fistula, malignancy, or structural abnormality is suspected
redFlags: Associated haematuria requiring exclusion of urinary tract malignancy
New incontinence with neurological signs suggesting cord compression or cauda equina syndrome
Overflow incontinence from unrecognised chronic retention with risk of renal impairment
Continuous leakage suggesting a urinary fistula
Recurrent urinary infection or significant post-void residual
reference.prognosis: Many patients improve substantially with conservative measures and correction of reversible factors; stress and urgency incontinence respond well to targeted therapy, and surgery offers durable benefit for refractory stress incontinence, though outcomes vary with cause and comorbidity.
pitfalls: Mislabelling overflow incontinence as urgency and prescribing antimuscarinics that worsen retention
Failing to measure post-void residual before treating
Overlooking reversible causes such as infection, medications, or stool impaction
Missing haematuria or a neurological cause behind new incontinence
Recommending surgery without adequate assessment of the incontinence type
management: Classify the incontinence type and correct reversible contributors, advising weight loss, caffeine and fluid moderation, and treatment of constipation

Treat stress incontinence first with supervised pelvic floor muscle training, adding duloxetine as an adjunct and reserving mid-urethral sling, colposuspension or urethral bulking agents, and an artificial urinary sphincter after prostatectomy, for refractory cases
Treat urgency incontinence and overactive bladder with bladder retraining plus an antimuscarinic or a beta-3 agonist such as mirabegron
Escalate refractory urgency incontinence to intravesical botulinum toxin, percutaneous tibial nerve stimulation, or sacral neuromodulation
Manage overflow incontinence by relieving outlet obstruction and using clean intermittent self-catheterisation for an underactive or neurogenic detrusor
Provide containment aids and skin care, and refer for urodynamic assessment in complex, mixed, neurogenic or pre-surgical cases
